questions.stemText:
The nuclear fission reaction of Uranium-235 may be represented by the following equation

$\vphantom{U}^{235}_{92}\mathrm{U} + {}^{1}_{0}\mathrm{n} \rightarrow {}^{141}_{56}\mathrm{Ba} + {}^{92}_{36}\mathrm{Kr} + 3\,{}^{1}_{0}\mathrm{n} + \text{energy}$

The rest masses of the nuclei are

nuclide | rest mass
$\vphantom{U}^{235}_{92}\mathrm{U}$ | $235.04393\ \mathrm{u}$
$\vphantom{B}^{141}_{56}\mathrm{Ba}$ | $140.91440\ \mathrm{u}$
$\vphantom{K}^{92}_{36}\mathrm{Kr}$ | $91.92617\ \mathrm{u}$
$\vphantom{n}^{1}_{0}\mathrm{n}$ | $1.00866\ \mathrm{u}$

What is the energy released when one nuclide of $\vphantom{U}^{235}_{92}\mathrm{U}$ undergoes fission?

A $3.09\times10^{-28}\ \mathrm{J}$
B $9.26\times10^{-20}\ \mathrm{J}$
C $2.78\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{J}$
D $3.29\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{J}$

stemImage.alt: Question 29: The nuclear fission reaction of Uranium-235 may be represented by the following equation 235 141 92 1 → 1 + energy U + n Ba + Kr + 3 n 92 56 36 0 0 The rest mas

questions.difficultyReason: The student must account for all neutron masses, convert units and apply mass–energy equivalence.
questions.misconception: Omitting free neutrons from the mass balance

explanation.body: Subtract the total product mass from the total reactant mass to get $\Delta m=[(235.04393+1.00866)-(140.91440+91.92617+3\times1.00866)]\ \mathrm{u}$. This is $3.088\times10^{-28}\ \mathrm{kg}$. The energy released is $E=(\Delta m)c^2=2.78\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{J}$.

perOption.A: Reports the mass difference in kilograms as an energy in joules.
perOption.B: Multiplies the mass difference by the speed of light only once.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Omits the three outgoing neutrons from the product mass.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
The graph below shows the variation with time t of the natural logarithm of the count rate

ln C of a radioactive source measured by a Geiger–Müller counter.

What is the half-life of the radioactive source?
questions.stemText: The graph below shows the variation with time t of the natural logarithm of the count rate ln C of a radioactive source measured by a Geiger–Müller counter. ln (C / s−1) 6 4 2 t / s 0 0 10 20 30 What is the half-life of the radioactive source? A 0.2 s B 3.5 s C 13 s D 26 s
questions.difficultyReason: The student must obtain the decay constant from the logarithmic plot before calculating the half-life.
questions.misconception: Halving the logarithm instead of the count rate

explanation.body: The graph of $\ln C$ against $t$ is linear, with gradient $(0-5.20)/(26.0-0)=-0.20\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$. The gradient is $-\lambda$, so $t_{1/2}=\ln 2/\lambda=\ln 2/0.20=3.5\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: Reports the magnitude of the gradient, which is the decay constant in inverse seconds.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Reads the time for the logarithm of the count rate to halve.
perOption.D: Reads the time intercept, where the count rate is one count per second.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
In the Rutherford $\alpha$-particle scattering experiment, $\alpha$-particles are directed at a thin gold foil.

Which is a direct deduction from the results of the experiment?

A The $\alpha$-particles are negatively charged.
B The $\alpha$-particles are positively charged.
C The atom consists of a large amount of empty space.
D The proton number of the gold nucleus is 79.

stemImage.alt: Question 29: In the Rutherford - particle scattering experiment, - particles are directed at a thin gold foil. Which is a direct deduction from the results of the experime

appearances.originalFile: grail:10416 ACJC 2023 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: It asks for the standard inference from most alpha particles passing through the foil.
questions.misconception: Confusing known projectile properties with experimental deductions

explanation.body: Most alpha particles passed through the thin foil with little or no deflection. The rare large deflections show that the region producing strong scattering occupies very little of each atom, so most of the atom is empty space.

perOption.A: Alpha particles are positively charged.
perOption.B: The positive charge of the incident alpha particles was already known.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: The observation that most particles pass through does not determine gold’s exact proton number.

questions.difficultyReason: The student must convert binding energy per nucleon to total binding energy and take the difference.
questions.misconception: Comparing binding energies per nucleon without tracking the nuclei

explanation.body: The energy released is the increase in total binding energy, and free neutrons contribute zero binding energy. For the two product nuclei and the original uranium nucleus, this gives $92(8.70)+141(8.33)-235(7.59)=191.28\ \mathrm{MeV}$, or $191\ \mathrm{MeV}$ to three significant figures.

perOption.A: Accounts for only part of the change in binding energy, which requires both product nuclei and the full uranium contribution.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
The Rutherford scattering experiment found that most of the alpha-particles passed through the gold foil with no significant deviation, although a very tiny minority were deflected through large angles, and some were even back-scattered.

The experiment is repeated with a foil made from a heavier isotope of gold.

How would the results be different?
questions.stemText: The Rutherford scattering experiment found that most of the alpha-particles passed through the gold foil with no significant deviation, although a very tiny minority were deflected through large angles, and some were even back-scattered. The experiment is repeated with a foil made from a heavier isotope of gold. How would the results be different? A There would be no significant change. B A much greater proportion of the alpha-particles would be back-scattered. C A much greater proportion of the alpha-particles would be deflected through a large angle. D A greater proportion of the alpha-particles would pass through with no significant deviation.

options.label: A
options.text: There would be no significant change.

options.label: B
options.text: A much greater proportion of the alpha-particles would be back-scattered.

options.label: C
options.text: A much greater proportion of the alpha-particles would be deflected through a large angle.

options.label: D
options.text: A greater proportion of the alpha-particles would pass through with no significant deviation.

appearances.originalFile: grail:14529 (ACJC) 2024 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student applies the unchanged nuclear charge of an isotope to Rutherford scattering.
questions.misconception: Assuming extra neutrons increase nuclear charge

explanation.body: Most alpha particles still pass through with negligible deviation because atoms are mainly empty space. The heavier isotope has the same nuclear charge, and the chance of a nearly head-on encounter is approximately unchanged. The scattering pattern therefore shows no significant change.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Extra neutrons leave the nuclear charge and the chance of near-head-on scattering essentially unchanged.
perOption.C: The higher nuclear mass does not substantially strengthen the Coulomb repulsion responsible for large deflections.
perOption.D: Changing the isotope does not appreciably change the chance of an encounter that deflects an alpha particle.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A nucleus of element X absorbs a neutron and undergoes nuclear fission to give a nucleus of element Y and a nucleus of element Z.

Which row gives the correct relation of the binding energy per nucleon of the respective nuclei?

Option | (binding energy per nucleon of Y) / (binding energy per nucleon of X) | (total binding energy per nucleon of Y and Z) / (binding energy per nucleon of X)
A | greater than 1 | greater than 1
B | greater than 1 | less than 1
C | less than 1 | greater than 1
D | less than 1 | less than 1

stemImage.alt: Question 30: A nucleus of element X absorbs a neutron and undergoes nuclear fission to give a nucleus of element Y and a nucleus of element Z. Which row gives the correct re

appearances.originalFile: grail:14529 (ACJC) 2024 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student uses the relation between binding energy per nucleon and stability to compare the nuclei.
questions.misconception: Assuming the heavier parent is more tightly bound per nucleon

explanation.body: The fission products Y and Z are more stable than X. Each therefore has a higher binding energy per nucleon than X, so both ratios in row A exceed 1.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Both products have greater binding energy per nucleon than X, so the second ratio also exceeds 1.
perOption.C: Y has greater binding energy per nucleon than X, so the first ratio exceeds 1.
perOption.D: Reverses the binding-energy-per-nucleon comparison for the parent and its fission products.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
Which observation shows that a radioactive source emits only $\alpha$-radiation?

A. The count rate reduces significantly 1 cm away from the source in air.
B. The count rate reduces significantly when the source is surrounded by a lead block.
C. The radiation beam is deflected by an electric field perpendicular to it.
D. The radiation beam remains undeflected by a magnetic field parallel to it.

stemImage.alt: Question 30: Which observation shows that a radioactive source emits only α-radiation?

appearances.originalFile: grail:19926 ACJC 2025 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The intended answer relies on recognising the short range of alpha radiation in air.
questions.misconception: Treating electric deflection as unique to alpha particles

explanation.body: The key selects the large drop in count rate over $1\ \mathrm{cm}$ of air because alpha radiation has a short range in air. Beta and gamma radiation are more penetrating, so the key uses the short-distance drop as the distinguishing observation.

perOption.A: Correct. Alpha radiation has a short range in air.
perOption.B: A lead block can shield alpha, beta and gamma radiation.
perOption.C: Both alpha and beta particles are charged and deflect in a perpendicular electric field.
perOption.D: A magnetic field parallel to the beam leaves alpha, beta and gamma radiation undeflected.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
The activity of a radioactive sample decreases to one third of its original activity $A_{o}$ in a period of 3 years.

What is the activity of the sample after another 3 years?
questions.stemText: The activity of a radioactive sample decreases to one third of its original activity Ao in a period of 3 years. What is the activity of the sample after another 3 years? A 0.11 $A_{o}$ B 0.17 $A_{o}$ C 0.33 $A_{o}$ D 0.67 $A_{o}$

appearances.originalFile: ACJC Physics/H2/2026 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1 sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Recognise that equal time intervals multiply activity by the same factor.
questions.misconception: Treating exponential decay as linear

explanation.body: For radioactive decay, $A=A_0e^{-\lambda t}$. At three years, $A_0/3=A_0e^{-3\lambda}$, so $\lambda=\ln(1/3)/(-3)=0.36620\ \mathrm{yr}^{-1}$. At six years, $A=A_0e^{-0.36620(6)}\approx0.11A_0$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Treats the second three-year interval as one half-life.
perOption.C: Gives the activity after only three years.
perOption.D: Gives the fraction lost in the first three years.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
In repeating Rutherford’s alpha particle scattering experiment, a student used the apparatus shown, in a vacuum, to determine n the number of alpha particles incident per unit time on a detector held at various angular positions θ.

Which graph best represents the variation of n with θ?
questions.stemText: In repeating Rutherford’s alpha particle scattering experiment, a student used the apparatus shown, in a vacuum, to determine n the number of alpha particles incident per unit time on a detector held at various angular positions θ. Which graph best represents the variation of n with θ? A n θ / ° -170 -90 0 +90 +170 B n θ / ° -170 -90 0 +90 +170 C n θ / ° -170 -90 0 +90 +170 D n θ / ° -170 -90 0 +90 +170
questions.difficultyReason: The student must translate the Rutherford scattering result into an angular count-rate graph.
questions.misconception: Overestimating the frequency of backscattering

explanation.body: Most alpha particles pass through the foil undeflected, so $n$ peaks sharply at $0^\circ$. Very few particles are deflected through large angles, so the count rate stays low at large positive and negative angles.

perOption.A: This puts the highest rates near backscattering angles and misses the strong undeviated beam.
perOption.B: This gives backscattering peaks comparable to the forward peak even though backscattering is rare.
perOption.C: Correct. A narrow forward peak dominates the low counts at large angles.
perOption.D: The broad peak implies too many particles are scattered through intermediate angles.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Today, the activity of a sample of caesium−137 is 4.0 x $10^{5}$ Bq. The half-life of caesium−137 is 33 years.

What is the best estimate of the number of caesium−137 nuclei that will decay in the next two days?
questions.stemText: Today, the activity of a sample of caesium−137 is 4.0 x 105 Bq. The half-life of caesium−137 is 33 years. What is the best estimate of the number of caesium−137 nuclei that will decay in the next two days? A 5.0 x $10^{8}$ B 1.2 x $10^{9}$ C 6.9 x $10^{10}$ D 9.5 x $10^{12}$

appearances.originalFile: grail:18733 ASRJC 2025 Prelim P1 H2 Physics QN paper

questions.difficultyReason: The student must justify constant activity over two days and convert the duration to seconds.
questions.misconception: Using becquerels with a duration in days

explanation.body: Two days is very short compared with the 33-year half-life, so the activity is effectively constant. Activity is the number of decays per unit time, giving $N_{\mathrm{decay}}\approx At=(4.0\times10^5)(2\times24\times3600)=6.912\times10^{10}$ decays.

perOption.A: This undercounts the decays by using an effective duration far shorter than two days.
perOption.B: This is close to what results from using the number of minutes in two days as the number of seconds.
perOption.C: Correct. The activity times the elapsed seconds gives about 69 billion decays.
perOption.D: This would require a much larger activity or a much longer time than given.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
The rest-masses of deuteron ${}^{2}_{1}\mathrm{H}$, proton and neutron are $2.0150\ \mathrm{u}$, $1.0086\ \mathrm{u}$ and $1.0097\ \mathrm{u}$ respectively. Which one of the following reactions takes place so that the deuteron may disintegrate to a proton and neutron?

A Releasing a photon of energy $2\ \mathrm{MeV}$.
B Releasing a photon of energy $3\ \mathrm{MeV}$.
C Capturing a photon of energy $2\ \mathrm{MeV}$.
D Capturing a photon of energy $3\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

stemImage.alt: Question 29: The rest-masses of deuteron 2 1H , proton and neutron are 2.0150 u, 1.0086 u and 1.0097 u respectively. Which one of the following reactions takes place so that

appearances.originalFile: grail:14523 ASRJC 2024 JC2 H2 Physics Prelim P1
grail:19921 SAJC Prelim H2 P1 2025_Qn and Ans

questions.difficultyReason: The student must compare rest masses and convert the mass difference to an energy threshold.
questions.misconception: Confusing binding energy with energy released during breakup

explanation.body: The combined rest mass of the proton and neutron exceeds that of the deuteron, so the reaction needs an energy input. The mass difference is $(1.0086+1.0097-2.0150)\ \mathrm{u}=0.0033\ \mathrm{u}$. Using $E=\Delta mc^2$ gives about $3.07\ \mathrm{MeV}$, rounded to $3\ \mathrm{MeV}$ in the key.

perOption.A: Photon emission takes energy away from a reaction that requires energy input.
perOption.B: Even a 3 MeV emitted photon would carry energy away from the breakup.
perOption.C: A 2 MeV photon supplies less than the binding energy.
perOption.D: Correct under the key’s rounding to whole MeV.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: Which combination of successive emissions produces a final nucleus with the same proton number as the starting nucleus?
questions.stemText: Which combination of successive emissions produces a final nucleus with the same proton number as the starting nucleus? A α α β B α β β C α β γ D β γ β

appearances.originalFile: grail:14523 ASRJC 2024 JC2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student must add the proton-number changes associated with successive emissions.
questions.misconception: Reversing the proton-number change in beta-minus decay

explanation.body: Alpha decay decreases the proton number by 2, beta-minus decay increases it by 1, and gamma emission leaves it unchanged. One alpha emission followed by two beta-minus emissions gives a net change of $-2+1+1=0$.

perOption.A: Two alpha emissions and one beta-minus emission give a net change of −3.
perOption.B: Correct. The changes cancel.
perOption.C: One alpha and one beta-minus emission give a net change of −1, and gamma emission leaves it unchanged.
perOption.D: Two beta-minus emissions raise the proton number by 2, and gamma emission leaves it unchanged.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A nucleus X decays into a nucleus Y by emitting an alpha particle followed by two beta particles.

Which statement about this nuclear decay is correct?
questions.stemText: A nucleus X decays into a nucleus Y by emitting an alpha particle followed by two beta particles. Which statement about this nuclear decay is correct? A Beta particle decay occurs when an orbital electron is emitted. B Nucleus Y has the same nucleon number as nucleus X. C Nucleus Y is an isotope of nucleus X. D The total mass of the products is equal to the mass of the initial nucleus X.

options.label: A
options.text: Beta particle decay occurs when an orbital electron is emitted.

options.label: B
options.text: Nucleus Y has the same nucleon number as nucleus X.

options.label: C
options.text: Nucleus Y is an isotope of nucleus X.

options.label: D
options.text: The total mass of the products is equal to the mass of the initial nucleus X.

appearances.originalFile: grail:18733 ASRJC 2025 Prelim P1 H2 Physics QN paper

questions.difficultyReason: Tracks proton and nucleon numbers through three emissions.
questions.misconception: Confusing proton number with nucleon number

explanation.body: The key tracks the charged products using $\vphantom{X}{}^{a}_{b}\mathrm{X}\to{}^{a-4}_{b}\mathrm{Y}+{}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}+2\,{}^{0}_{-1}\mathrm{e}$. X and Y have the same proton number and different neutron numbers, so Y is an isotope of X.

perOption.A: A beta-minus electron is produced when a neutron in the nucleus becomes a proton.
perOption.B: Alpha emission lowers the daughter nucleus's nucleon number by four.
perOption.C: Correct. Y has the same proton number and four fewer neutrons.
perOption.D: The products carry kinetic energy, so their total rest mass is smaller.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: Nucleus P decays in two stages to produce nucleus Q. Which decay sequence will result in the highest number of neutrons in nucleus Q? A a $\beta$-particle followed by a $\gamma$-ray B an $\alpha$-particle followed by a $\gamma$-ray C an $\alpha$-particle followed by a $\beta$-particle D a $\beta$-particle followed by another $\beta$-particle

stemImage.alt: Question 29: Nucleus P decays in two stages to produce nucleus Q. Which decay sequence will result in the highest number of neutrons in nucleus Q?

appearances.originalFile: ASRJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1 for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Tracking the neutron number change for each decay type.
questions.misconception: Thinking β-decay leaves the neutron number unchanged or that γ emission changes the nucleus composition

explanation.body: Let R be the intermediate nucleus. Beta decay gives $\phantom{}^{A}_{Z}\mathrm{P}\to{}^{A}_{Z+1}\mathrm{R}+{}^{0}_{-1}\mathrm{e}$, followed by gamma decay $\phantom{}^{A}_{Z+1}\mathrm{R}\to{}^{A}_{Z+1}\mathrm{Q}+\gamma$. The neutron number in Q is $A-(Z+1)=A-Z-1$.

perOption.A: Correct. The neutron count drops by just one.
perOption.B: Alpha decay removes two neutrons and gamma emission leaves the neutron count unchanged.
perOption.C: Alpha decay removes two neutrons and beta-minus decay converts one more into a proton.
perOption.D: Each beta-minus decay converts a neutron to a proton, so the count drops by two.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A radioactive source is placed near a detector and the reading is 324 counts per minute. After two half-lives, the reading drops to 108 counts per minute.

What is the background radiation in counts per minute?
questions.stemText: A radioactive source is placed near a detector and the reading is 324 counts per minute. After two half-lives, the reading drops to 108 counts per minute. What is the background radiation in counts per minute? A 27 B 36 C 54 D 72

appearances.originalFile: ASRJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1 for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires separating the constant background from the decaying source count over two half-lives.
questions.misconception: Halving the total count rate, including background, each half-life

explanation.body: Let $C$ be the initial count rate due to the source alone. After two half-lives it has fallen by $3C/4$, so $3C/4=324-108$ and $C=288\ \mathrm{counts\,min^{-1}}$. The background count rate is $324-288=36\ \mathrm{counts\,min^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Quarters the later reading even though it includes a constant background contribution.
perOption.B: Correct. The background contributes 36 counts per minute.
perOption.C: Halves the later reading even though the half-life applies only to the source contribution.
perOption.D: Gives the remaining source count rate after two half-lives.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
One nuclear reaction that can take place in a nuclear reactor may be represented by the equation

${}^{235}_{92}\mathrm{U}+{}^{1}_{0}\mathrm{n}\rightarrow{}^{95}_{42}\mathrm{Mo}+{}^{139}_{57}\mathrm{La}+2\,{}^{1}_{0}\mathrm{n}+7\,{}^{0}_{-1}\mathrm{e}$

Data for a nucleus and some particles are given in the table.

nucleus or particle | mass / u
${}^{139}_{57}\mathrm{La}$ nucleus | 138.955
${}^{1}_{0}\mathrm{n}$ particle | 1.00863
${}^{1}_{1}\mathrm{p}$ particle | 1.00728
${}^{0}_{-1}\mathrm{e}$ particle | $5.49\times10^{-4}$

What is the binding energy per nucleon of lanthanum-139 (${}^{139}_{57}\mathrm{La}$)?

A 7.84 Mev
B 7.87 MeV
C 19.13 MeV
D 19.19 MeV

stemImage.alt: Question 29: One nuclear reaction that can take place in a nuclear reactor may be represented by the equation 235 1 95 139 1 0 U n Mo La 2 n 7 e + → + + + 57 0 1 92 0 42 − D

questions.difficultyReason: The student must find the nuclear mass defect, convert it to energy, and divide by the nucleon count.
questions.misconception: Confusing proton number with nucleon number

explanation.body: Use the given nuclear mass to find the mass defect: $\Delta m=[82(1.00863)+57(1.00728)-138.955]\ \mathrm{u}=1.16762\ \mathrm{u}$. The binding energy is $\Delta mc^2=(1.16762)(1.66\times10^{-27})(3.00\times10^8)^2=1.74442428\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{J}$, or $1090.265\ \mathrm{MeV}$ using $1\ \mathrm{MeV}=1.60\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{J}$. Dividing by $139$ gives $7.84\ \mathrm{MeV}$ per nucleon.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Including the seven electron masses inflates the nuclear mass defect.
perOption.C: Divides the binding energy by 57 protons instead of 139 nucleons.
perOption.D: Includes the seven electron masses and divides by the proton count.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
The half-life of a certain radioactive isotope is 32 hours.

What fraction of a sample would remain after 16 hours?
questions.stemText: The half-life of a certain radioactive isotope is 32 hours. What fraction of a sample would remain after 16 hours? A 0.25 B 0.29 C 0.5 D 0.71
questions.difficultyReason: The student must apply the decay factor for half of a half-life.
questions.misconception: Confusing fraction decayed with fraction remaining

explanation.body: Use $x=x_0(\tfrac12)^n$, where $n$ is the number of elapsed half-lives. In $16$ hours, $n=16/32=0.5$, so $x=x_0(\tfrac12)^{0.5}=0.7071x_0\approx0.71x_0$.

perOption.A: Treats 16 hours as two half-lives by reversing the time ratio.
perOption.B: Gives the fraction that decayed.
perOption.C: Gives the fraction remaining after a full half-life.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A nuclear fusion reaction is as follows:

$^{7}_{3}\mathrm{Li}+{}^{1}_{1}\mathrm{H}\to2\,{}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}$

The masses of the nuclei are as follow:
$^{7}_{3}\mathrm{Li}$: $7.018\,\mathrm{u}$
$^{1}_{1}\mathrm{H}$: $1.008\,\mathrm{u}$
$^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}$: $4.004\,\mathrm{u}$

What is the amount of energy released in this reaction?
A $9.0\times10^{-21}\ \mathrm{J}$
B $2.7\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{J}$
C $6.0\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{J}$
D $1.6\times10^{15}\ \mathrm{J}$

stemImage.alt: Question 29: A nuclear fusion reaction is as follows: 1 7 1H → 2 4 3Li + 2He The masses of the nuclei are as follow: 7 3Li: 7.018u 1 1H: 1.008u 4 2He : 4.004u What is the am

questions.difficultyReason: Subtract the product mass, convert the mass difference to kilograms and apply mass–energy equivalence.
questions.misconception: Forgetting the two helium nuclei

explanation.body: The energy released is the difference between the reactant and product masses multiplied by $c^2$. Substituting gives $[(7.018+1.008)-2(4.004)](1.66\times10^{-27})(3.00\times10^8)^2=2.6892\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{J}$, which rounds to $2.7\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{J}$.

perOption.A: Uses $c$ instead of $c^2$.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Counts only one helium nucleus in the products.
perOption.D: Uses the numerical mass difference in atomic mass units as though it were in kilograms.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
$^{218}\mathrm{Po}$ decays to $^{214}\mathrm{Bi}$ via two pathways as shown in the figure below.

[Upper pathway: $^{218}\mathrm{Po}$ goes to Pb via X, then to $^{214}\mathrm{Bi}$ via $\beta$ decay. Lower pathway: $^{218}\mathrm{Po}$ goes to At via Y, then to $^{214}\mathrm{Bi}$ via Z.]

What are the possible radioactive decay modes X, Y and Z?

Option | X | Y | Z
A | $\gamma$ decay | $\alpha$ decay | $\beta$ decay
B | $\alpha$ decay | $\beta$ decay | $\alpha$ decay
C | $\beta$ decay | $\alpha$ decay | $\gamma$ decay
D | $\alpha$ decay | $\alpha$ decay | $\beta$ decay

stemImage.alt: Question 30: 218Po decays to 214Bi via two pathways as shown in the figure below. X 훽 decay Y Z What are the possible radioactive decay modes X, Y and Z? X Y Z

questions.difficultyReason: Follow the two pathways and track changes in mass number and element.
questions.misconception: Confusing the effects of alpha and beta decay

explanation.body: The $\beta$ decay from Pb to $^{214}\mathrm{Bi}$ leaves the mass number unchanged, so X must account for the drop from 218 to 214. An $\alpha$ particle is a $^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}$ nucleus and carries away four nucleons, ruling out A and C. If Y were $\alpha$ decay, its daughter would be Pb, ruling out D.

perOption.A: A $\gamma$ decay at X cannot account for the decrease of four in mass number.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: A $\beta$ decay at X leaves the mass number unchanged.
perOption.D: An $\alpha$ decay at Y would produce Pb in place of At.

explanation.body: Oxygen-28 has 8 protons and 20 neutrons, while calcium-40 has 20 of each, so both are doubly magic. Iron-56 has 26 protons and 30 neutrons, nickel-50 has 28 and 22, and tin-126 has 50 and 76. None of these last three has two magic counts, so the total is 2.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
In the following induced nuclear reaction, when one Lithium-7 nucleus reacts with one Hydrogen-1 nucleus, X number of Helium-4 nuclei are produced.

${}^{7}_{3}\mathrm{Li}+{}^{1}_{1}\mathrm{H}\to X({}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He})+\text{energy}$

During the reaction, $1.6\times10^{12}\ \mathrm{J}$ of energy is released when $1.0\ \mathrm{g}$ of Hydrogen-1 (mass of 1 Hydrogen-1 nucleus $=1.008\ \mathrm{u}$) and sufficient Lithium-7 are used. The binding energy of a Helium-4 nucleus is $28.3\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

What is the binding energy of a Lithium-7 nucleus?

A $11.6\ \mathrm{MeV}$
B $39.9\ \mathrm{MeV}$
C $56.6\ \mathrm{MeV}$
D $68.2\ \mathrm{MeV}$

stemImage.alt: Question 29: In the following induced nuclear reaction, when one Lithium-7 nucleus reacts with one Hydrogen-1 nucleus, X number of Helium-4 nuclei are produced. ( ) 7 1 4 Li

questions.difficultyReason: The student must balance the reaction, convert bulk energy to energy per reaction and compare binding energies.
questions.misconception: Confusing binding energy with released energy

explanation.body: Conservation of charge and nucleon number gives $X=2$. There are $0.001/(1.008\times1.66\times10^{-27})=5.98\times10^{23}$ hydrogen nuclei. The energy released per reaction is $1.6\times10^{12}/[(5.98\times10^{23})(1.6\times10^{-13})]=16.73\ \mathrm{MeV}$. Hydrogen-1 is a single proton with zero binding energy, so $2(28.3)-B_{\mathrm{Li}}=16.73$ in MeV. Thus $B_{\mathrm{Li}}=39.9\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

perOption.A: This subtracts the energy released from the binding energy of only one helium nucleus.
perOption.B: Correct. Both helium nuclei contribute to the products’ binding energy.
perOption.C: This gives just the products’ total binding energy.
perOption.D: This exceeds the products’ total binding energy, which would require an energy input.

questions.stemText:
Nuclide X decays to stable nuclide Y with a half-life of $T$ years.

Geologists discovered that nuclide Y found in a particular rock sample all came from nuclide X which was present when the rock was formed.

The rock is thought to be $3T$ years old.

What is the expected ratio $\frac{\text{number of atoms of X}}{\text{number of atoms of Y}}$ for this rock?

A $\frac{1}{2}$
B $\frac{1}{3}$
C $\frac{1}{6}$
D $\frac{1}{7}$

stemImage.alt: Question 30: Nuclide X decays to stable nuclide Y with a half-life of T years. Geologists discovered that nuclide Y found in a particular rock sample all came from nuclide X

questions.difficultyReason: The remaining parent fraction must be compared with the fraction that decayed.
questions.misconception: Using initial parent count for daughter count

explanation.body: After $3T$, the surviving X count is $(1/2)^{3T/T}N_0=N_0/8$. The other $7N_0/8$ atoms have become Y, so $N_X/N_Y=(N_0/8)/(7N_0/8)=1/7$.

perOption.A: This uses the fraction of X remaining after just one half-life.
perOption.B: The number of half-lives determines how many times to halve the count.
perOption.C: This undercounts Y: seven of every eight initial X nuclei decay.
perOption.D: Correct. The ratio is $1/7$.

The binding energies per nucleon are:
for $\vphantom{H}^2_1\mathrm{H}$, $1.09\ \mathrm{MeV}$,
for $\vphantom{H}^3_2\mathrm{He}$, $2.54\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

How much energy is released in this reaction?

A $0.36\ \mathrm{MeV}$
B $1.45\ \mathrm{MeV}$
C $3.26\ \mathrm{MeV}$

questions.difficultyReason: Convert the binding energies per nucleon to total binding energies.
questions.misconception: Using binding energy per nucleon as total binding energy

explanation.body: The energy released equals the total binding energy of the products minus that of the reactants. The free neutron contributes zero binding energy, so the difference is $3(2.54)-2[2(1.09)]=3.26\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

perOption.A: Subtracts the two deuterium per-nucleon values from the helium per-nucleon value.
perOption.B: Subtracts the binding energies per nucleon directly.

questions.misconception: Equating the mass lost with the fraction of nuclei decayed

explanation.body: Starting with $N$ nuclei, $3N/4$ decay in two half-lives. Approximating nuclear masses by their nucleon numbers in atomic mass units, the change is $\Delta m=[-(3N/4)(210)+(3N/4)(206)]\,\mathrm u=-3N\,\mathrm u$. The masses of the nuclides involved are as follows

[Table headed nuclide and mass / $u$.]

${}^{1}_{1}\mathrm H$ 1.007825

Nuclide C has a half-life of 5 years, while nuclide N has a half-life of 90 years. The activity $A$ of a mixture of C and N is measured.

Which graph best represents the variation with time $t$ of the natural logarithm of $A$?

[All graphs have vertical axis $\ln A$ and horizontal axis $t$.]
A [Increasing curve, steep at first and then gentler.]
B [Decreasing curve, gentle at first and then steeper.]
C [Increasing curve, gentle at first and then steeper.]
D [Decreasing curve, steep at first and then gentler.]

stemImage.alt: Question 29: Nuclide C has a half-life of 5 years, while nuclide N has a half-life of 90 years. The activity A of a mixture of C and N is measured. Which graph best represen

questions.difficultyReason: Students must interpret logarithmic slopes and reason about how two decay contributions change relative to each other.
questions.misconception: Assuming the shorter-lived nuclide dominates at late times

explanation.body: For either nuclide, $A=A_0e^{-\lambda t}$ and $\lambda=\ln2/t_{1/2}$, so $\lambda_C>\lambda_N$. Taking logs gives $\ln A=\ln A_0-\lambda t$, a straight line with gradient $-\lambda$ for each nuclide. If C dominates initially, the mixture starts with a gradient close to $-\lambda_C$. As C decays away, N dominates and the gradient approaches the gentler $-\lambda_N$.

perOption.A: Shows rising activity even though both components decay.
perOption.B: Makes the decay slope steeper with time, although the faster-decaying contribution shrinks.
perOption.C: Shows rising activity with an increasingly positive slope.
perOption.D: Correct. The downward slope becomes gentler as N contributes a larger fraction of the activity.

After four half-lives have elapsed, the total count rate decreases to one-quarter of its initial value. What is the background count rate? A 0 counts $\mathrm{min}^{-1}$ B 13 counts $\mathrm{min}^{-1}$ C 40 counts $\mathrm{min}^{-1}$ D 50 counts $\mathrm{min}^{-1}$

appearances.originalFile: grail:26791 EJC 2026 JC2 H2 PHYSICS PRELIM P1

questions.difficultyReason: Requires distinguishing total and net counts and solving an equation after four halvings.
questions.misconception: Applying radioactive decay to the background contribution

explanation.body: Let $B$ be the background count rate, so the initial sample count rate is $200-B$. After four half-lives, the total is $0.25(200)=50$, giving a sample count rate of $50-B$. The sample count rate falls by a factor of $16$, so $\frac{50-B}{200-B}=(\frac12)^4=\frac1{16}$. Thus $800-16B=200-B$, giving $B=40\ \mathrm{counts\,min^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Assumes there is no background, which would give a final total of only $12.5\ \mathrm{counts\,min^{-1}}$.
perOption.B: Divides the initial total by 16 and mistakes the result for the background.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Treats the final total as pure background even though the sample is still contributing counts.

B. $1.73\ \mathrm{MeV}$

explanation.body: The energy released equals helium’s total binding energy minus the two deuterium nuclei’s total binding energy. If $b$ is the deuterium binding energy per nucleon in MeV, then $3.26=4(2.54)-4b$. Hence $b=1.725\ \mathrm{MeV}$, which rounds to $1.73\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

explanation.body: The range of beta-particle kinetic energies shows that the particles are emitted with a range of speeds. If the daughter nucleus and beta particle were the only products, energy and momentum conservation would fix both speeds for a given transition. The varying speeds indicate an additional particle that can carry energy and momentum.

questions.stemText: Which of the following statements concerning nuclear properties is true? A The greater the binding energy of a nucleus, the more stable it is. B If the total rest mass of the products of a reaction is greater than the total rest mass of the reactants, this reaction is impossible. C When a stationary nucleus decays by emitting a $\gamma$-photon, the nucleus will move off in an opposite direction to the photon. appearances.originalFile: MI Physics/H2/2026 PU3 H2 PHYSICS PRELIM P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Tests several subtle points: binding energy vs per nucleon, mass-energy in reactions, momentum conservation and decay independence.
questions.misconception: Judging nuclear stability by total binding energy rather than binding energy per nucleon

explanation.body: The total linear momentum is zero before the stationary nucleus emits the $\gamma$ photon. By conservation of linear momentum, the recoiling nucleus must have momentum equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the photon’s momentum.

perOption.A: Nuclear stability is compared using binding energy per nucleon rather than total binding energy.
perOption.B: A reaction with greater product rest mass can occur if enough energy is supplied to the reactants.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: In the usual nuclear-decay model, chemical reactions leave the half-life of the radionuclide unchanged.

questions.difficultyReason: Requires tracking the separate nucleon and proton number changes.
questions.misconception: Ignoring the proton-number increase in beta-minus decay

Which of the following nuclides will produce nuclide X by undergoing a series of decays to emit an alpha particle and two beta particles?

questions.misconception: Applying beta-minus decay with the wrong sign

explanation.body: The order of the decays does not affect the net change. One $\alpha$ decay and two $\beta^-$ decays give a net change of zero protons and a loss of four neutrons. The parent therefore has the same proton number as X and four more neutrons, which is point B.

perOption.A: Has two fewer protons than X, although the proton number is unchanged overall.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Has three extra protons and five extra neutrons, which do not match the net changes.

explanation.body: Let $N_0$ be the initial number of antimony nuclei. A ratio of one antimony nucleus to two tellurium nuclei means $N/N_0=1/3$. This fraction lies between $1/2$ after one half-life and $1/4$ after two half-lives, so the time is between 60 and 120 days.

questions.stemText: Two $\alpha$-particles with equal energies are fired towards the nucleus of a gold atom. Which diagram could represent their paths? questions.stemText: A radioactive source is placed 1 cm from a Geiger-Muller tube, and various absorbers are placed between them, one at a time. For each absorber, a one-minute count is taken of the total number of decays, and this is repeated several times. The table shows the results of the experiment. average number of decays absorber detected in one minute none 1043 0.1 mm paper 1040 1 mm aluminium 497 1 cm lead 6 The average background count per minute is 5. What nuclear radiation do the results suggest the source was emitting? A alpha and beta only B beta only C beta and gamma only D alpha, beta and gamma
questions.difficultyReason: Requires comparing each absorber count with the unshielded count and the background level.
questions.misconception: Taking every count above zero as evidence of source radiation

explanation.body: Paper barely changes the count, which gives little evidence of alpha radiation. The $1\ \mathrm{mm}$ aluminium absorbs some of the radiation, and the count with $1\ \mathrm{cm}$ of lead is 6 per minute, close to the background of 5 per minute. These observations suggest beta radiation only.

perOption.A: Paper would cause a noticeable decrease if alpha particles made an appreciable contribution.
perOption.B: Correct. The observed attenuation is consistent with beta radiation alone.
perOption.C: The count behind the lead is near background, giving little evidence of a penetrating gamma component.
perOption.D: The results give little evidence for alpha absorption by paper or for a gamma component above background behind lead.

questions.difficultyReason: Convert MeV to joules and use mass–energy equivalence with the correct sign.
questions.misconception: Forgetting the mega prefix or reversing the mass change

explanation.body: The released energy is $3.27\ \mathrm{MeV}=5.23\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{J}$. Its mass equivalent is $\Delta m=E/c^2=5.8\times10^{-30}\ \mathrm{kg}$. The reactants have the greater combined mass because the fusion releases energy.

questions.stem:
The beta spectrum for $^{12}$B decay is as shown below.

The kinetic energy of an emitted β-particle is 6.0 MeV. What is the approximate energy of the associated neutrino?
questions.stemText: The beta spectrum for 12B decay is as shown below. number of β-particles 0 6.0 0 13.4 kinetic energy of β-particle / MeV The kinetic energy of an emitted β-particle is 6.0 MeV. What is the approximate energy of the associated neutrino? A 4.0 MeV B 6.0 MeV C 7.4 MeV D 13.4 MeV
questions.difficultyReason: The student must identify the endpoint and subtract the beta particle’s share of the energy.
questions.misconception: Using the spectrum peak as the decay energy

explanation.body: The daughter nucleus takes negligible kinetic energy, so the beta particle and neutrino share the fixed energy released. The spectrum ends at $13.4\ \mathrm{MeV}$, where the beta particle takes essentially all of that energy. For a beta particle with $6.0\ \mathrm{MeV}$, the neutrino therefore takes $13.4-6.0=7.4\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

perOption.A: Using the peak of the spectrum confuses the most frequent beta energy with the energy available to share.
perOption.B: Uses the beta particle’s kinetic energy for the neutrino as well.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Assigns the full decay energy to the neutrino even though the beta particle carries $6.0\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: A radioactive source in the laboratory has a half-life of 10 days. The count rate was measured to be 100 Bq initially. 20 days later, the count rate was found to be 34 Bq. What is the count rate in the laboratory without the source?
questions.stemText: A radioactive source in the laboratory has a half-life of 10 days. The count rate was measured to be 100 Bq initially. 20 days later, the count rate was found to be 34 Bq. What is the count rate in the laboratory without the source? A 9 B 12 C 17 D 22
questions.difficultyReason: The student must subtract the same unknown background from both readings before applying two half-lives.
questions.misconception: Applying the half-life to the total measured rate

explanation.body: After 20 days, two half-lives have elapsed, so the source count rate is one quarter of its initial value. Subtracting the constant background $C_{\mathrm{bg}}$ from both measurements gives $34-C_{\mathrm{bg}}=\tfrac14(100-C_{\mathrm{bg}})$. Solving gives $C_{\mathrm{bg}}=12\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Applies the decay factor to the full initial reading and subtracts $25$ from $34$.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Halves the final measured rate without separating the source and background.
perOption.D: Divides the $66$ drop by three, which gives the source’s final contribution.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
The ratio of $^{14}$C : $^{12}$C in living things is fixed when they are alive but decreases after death because of the radioactive decay of $^{14}$C. $^{14}$C has a half-life of 5730 years. A 10.0 g sample of wood cut from a live tree is measured to have an activity of 120 $\mathrm{min}^{-1}$.

If a 1.0 g sample of an old wooden relic is found to have an activity of 8.05 $\mathrm{min}^{-1}$, how long ago was this wooden relic cut from a live tree?
questions.stemText: The ratio of 14C : 12C in living things is fixed when they are alive but decreases after death because of the radioactive decay of 14C. 14C has a half-life of 5730 years. A 10.0 g sample of wood cut from a live tree is measured to have an activity of 120 min−1. If a 1.0 g sample of an old wooden relic is found to have an activity of 8.05 min−1, how long ago was this wooden relic cut from a live tree? A 1470 years B 3300 years C 9950 years D 22300 years
questions.difficultyReason: Needs normalising activity per gram before applying exponential decay.
questions.misconception: Comparing activities without scaling for sample mass

explanation.body: Activity is proportional to the number of radioactive nuclei, so $1.0\ \mathrm{g}$ of live wood would have an activity of $120/10=12.0\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$. Using $A=A_0e^{-\lambda t}$ and $\lambda=\ln 2/5730\ \mathrm{yr}^{-1}$ gives $8.05=12.0e^{-(\ln 2)t/5730}$, with $t$ in years. Solving gives $t\approx3300$ years.

perOption.A: This age allows too little decay, leaving more than $8.05\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$ from a $12.0\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$ starting activity.
perOption.B: Correct. The mass-adjusted activity ratio gives about 3300 years.
perOption.C: Uses an age beyond one half-life even though more than half the initial activity remains.
perOption.D: Compares the activities directly without adjusting for the tenfold difference in sample mass.

A 6.7 B 6.8 C 8.4 D 8.5

questions.difficultyReason: Needs energy release as the increase in total binding energy, counting nucleons correctly.
questions.misconception: Including free neutrons in the product binding energy

explanation.body: The energy released equals the products’ total binding energy minus the reactants’ total binding energy. Free neutrons contribute zero binding energy, so $195=143X+90X-235(7.6)$, with energies in MeV. Solving gives $X=8.50\ \mathrm{MeV}$ per nucleon.

perOption.A: Reverses the energy difference and also uses too many bound product nucleons.
perOption.B: Subtracts the released energy from the initial binding energy instead of adding it.
perOption.C: Averages over too many nucleons by counting free neutrons in the product binding-energy calculation.
perOption.D: Correct. The 195 MeV increase is shared across 233 bound product nucleons.

Which of the following graphs best represents the variation of the logarithm of the count-rate $C$ of the gases with time $t$?

[All four graphs plot $\ln C$ against $t$, mark $0$ and $T$, and show an upward jump at $T$.]
A. [The falling curve flattens before $T$ and again after the jump.]
B. [A falling straight line before $T$ is followed by a falling curve that progressively flattens.]
C. [A falling straight line before $T$ is followed by a steeper falling straight line.]
D. [A falling straight line before $T$ is followed by a shallower falling straight line.]

questions.difficultyReason: The student must interpret the logarithm of a count rate that combines two different exponential decays.
questions.misconception: Assuming the log of a sum of exponentials stays linear

explanation.body: Before $T$, $C=C_0e^{-\lambda t}$, giving $\ln C=\ln C_0-\lambda t$, a straight line of gradient $-\lambda$. At $T$, the added gas raises the count rate, and its larger decay constant makes the graph initially fall more steeply. As the faster-decaying gas contributes less, the gradient approaches its value before $T$.

perOption.A: Shows a curved logarithmic plot before $T$ even though only one gas is decaying.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Treats the post-injection count rate as a single exponential with a permanently steeper log slope.
perOption.D: Shows a shallower slope after injection even though the added gas decays faster.

questions.subject: h2-physics

questions.misconception: Assuming the daughter nuclei leave the sample

explanation.body: The sample still contains both the undecayed parent nuclei and the daughter nuclei. The emitted $\beta$ particles are electrons with masses much smaller than those of the parent nuclei, so the sample mass is only slightly less than $1\ \mathrm{g}$.

$^{235}_{92}\mathrm U$ | 7.60
$^{98}_{40}\mathrm{Zr}$ | 8.58
$^{136}_{52}\mathrm{Te}$ | 8.32

What is the energy released in the reaction?

A 186 MeV

questions.difficultyReason: The student must convert the three per-nucleon values to total binding energies and take the difference.
questions.misconception: Adding reactant and product binding energies

explanation.body: The energy released is the total binding energy of the products minus that of the reactants. Multiplying each binding energy per nucleon by its nuclide’s nucleon number gives $(8.32\times136)+(8.58\times98)-(7.60\times235)=186\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

perOption.A: Correct. The products gain about 186 MeV in total binding energy.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
The uranium nuclide $^{238}_{92}\mathrm U$ undergoes a series of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ decays to the stable lead nuclide $^{206}_{82}\mathrm{Pb}$.

What is the number of $\alpha$ decays and $\beta$ decays in the series of decays?

A 5 $\alpha$ decays and 12 $\beta$ decays
B 6 $\alpha$ decays and 8 $\beta$ decays
C 7 $\alpha$ decays and 4 $\beta$ decays
D 8 $\alpha$ decays and 6 $\beta$ decays

questions.difficultyReason: The student first balances nucleon number and then uses the alpha count to balance proton number.
questions.misconception: Assuming beta decay changes nucleon number

explanation.body: Let $m$ be the number of alpha decays and $n$ the number of beta-minus decays. Balancing nucleon numbers gives $4m+0=238-206$, so $m=8$. Balancing proton numbers gives $2m-n=92-82$, so $2(8)-n=10$ and $n=6$.

perOption.A: Five alpha decays remove only 20 nucleons.
perOption.B: Six alpha decays remove only 24 nucleons.
perOption.C: Seven alpha decays remove only 28 nucleons.
perOption.D: Correct. Eight alpha and six beta-minus decays balance both numbers.

explanation.body: The source alone initially gives $C_0=100-20=80\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$. In $60/20=3$ half-lives, its contribution drops to $(1/2)^3(80)=10\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$. Adding the background gives a recorded count-rate of $10+20=30\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$.

perOption.B: Applies three half-lives to the full initial count-rate, including background.

Which of the following occurs when a deuteron disintegrates into a proton and neutron?
A The deuteron emits a $\gamma$-ray photon of energy $2\ \mathrm{MeV}$.
B The deuteron captures a $\gamma$-ray photon of energy $2\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

explanation.body: The proton and neutron have combined rest energy $939+940=1879\ \mathrm{MeV}$. This exceeds the deuteron’s rest energy by $1879-1876=3\ \mathrm{MeV}$, so the deuteron must absorb a gamma photon of about $3\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A radioactive sample consists of two nuclides.

One has a half-life of $48\ \mathrm{h}$ and decays by emitting alpha particles, while the other has a half-life of $36\ \mathrm{h}$ and emits beta particles.

The initial count rate is $352\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$. When a sheet of paper is placed between the source and the detector, the count rate becomes $256\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$. The background count rate is $16\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$.

What will the count rate be after 6 days, without the paper present?

A. $27\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$
B. $36\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$
C. $43\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$
D. $52\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$

stemImage.alt: Question 29: A radioactive sample consists of two nuclides. One has a half-life of 48 h and decays by emitting alpha particles, while the other has a half-life of 36 h and e

questions.difficultyReason: Requires isolating two source rates, decaying them separately and restoring the background.
questions.misconception: Applying radioactive decay to background counts

explanation.body:
Paper stops alpha particles, so the initial alpha count rate is $352-256=96\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$ and the initial beta count rate is $256-16=240\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$. Six days is $144\ \mathrm{h}$, or three alpha half-lives and four beta half-lives.

The final alpha and beta count rates are $96/2^3=12\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$ and $240/2^4=15\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$. Adding the background gives $12+15+16=43\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Leaves out the background count at the detector.
perOption.B: Undercounts the source contribution, for example by applying too many half-lives.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Overcounts the source contribution by allowing too little decay.

Which explanation best explains the corresponding observation?

A Observation: Most of the particles undergo little to no deflection. Explanation: The electrostatic repulsion acting on them is only along the direction of initial velocity.
B Observation: Most of the particles undergo little to no deflection. Explanation: The mass of the nucleus is too little.
C Observation: A tiny fraction of the particles is scattered at large angles. Explanation: The nucleus is mostly empty space.

The nucleus contains most of the atom's mass and positive charge in a tiny region, so only a small fraction of the incident particles pass close enough to undergo such a deflection.

questions.stemText:
In the $\alpha$-particle scattering experiment, a beam of $\alpha$-particles is aimed at a thin gold foil. Most of the $\alpha$-particles go straight through or are deflected by a small angle. A very small proportion are deflected through more than $90^\circ$, effectively rebounding towards the source of the $\alpha$-particles.

Which conclusion about the structure of atoms cannot be drawn from this experiment alone?

A  Most of the atom is empty space.
B  Most of the mass of an atom is concentrated in the nucleus.
C  The nucleus contains both protons and neutrons.

questions.misconception: Inferring neutrons directly from Rutherford scattering

explanation.body: The scattering experiment reveals a small, massive, charged nucleus. The scattering observations do not reveal whether the nucleus contains neutrons, so they cannot establish that it contains both protons and neutrons.

perOption.A: Most alpha particles pass straight through or are only slightly deflected, which supports this inference.
perOption.B: The rare rebounds show that mass is concentrated in a small nucleus capable of deflecting an alpha particle through a large angle.

questions.stemText:
In a radioactive decay series, three successive decays each result in a particle being emitted.

The first decay results in the emission of a $\beta^-$ particle. The second decay results in the emission of an $\alpha$ particle. The third decay results in the emission of another $\beta^-$ particle.

[Decay diagram P → Q → R → S, with outgoing arrows labelled $\beta^-$ from P, $\alpha$ from Q and $\beta^-$ from R.]

Nuclides P and S are compared.

Which statement about S is correct?

A  S and P are identical in all respects.
B  S and P are isotopes of the same element.
C  S is a different element of a lower atomic number.
D  S is a different element of reduced mass.

questions.difficultyReason: Track both proton and nucleon numbers across the three successive decays.
questions.misconception: Tracking the alpha decay without both beta decays

explanation.body: Each $\beta^-$ decay increases the proton number by one and leaves the mass number unchanged. The $\alpha$ decay decreases the proton number by two and the mass number by four. Thus S has the same proton number as P and four fewer nucleons, making them isotopes of the same element.

perOption.A: The alpha decay leaves S with four fewer nucleons than P.

questions.stemText:
Nuclei of atoms can exist in excited states. When an excited nucleus returns to its state of lowest energy (the ground state), a $\gamma$-ray photon may be emitted.

The mass of a nucleus in its ground state is $59.9308\ \mathrm{u}$. The energy of the photon emitted when this nucleus returns from an excited state to the ground state is $2.13\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{J}$.

What is the mass of the nucleus in the excited state?

A $59.9208\ \mathrm{u}$
B $59.9294\ \mathrm{u}$
C $59.9322\ \mathrm{u}$
D $59.9337\ \mathrm{u}$

appearances.originalFile: grail:9648 SAJC 2022 Prelim P1 QP + Guide

questions.difficultyReason: It requires converting the photon energy to a mass difference in atomic mass units and choosing the correct sign.
questions.misconception: Subtracting the emitted photon’s mass equivalent from the ground-state mass

explanation.body: From $\Delta mc^2=E_\gamma$, the mass difference is $\Delta m=(2.13\times10^{-13})/(3.00\times10^8)^2=2.366667\times10^{-30}\ \mathrm{kg}$. Using $1\ \mathrm{u}=1.66\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}$ gives $\Delta m=0.0014257\ \mathrm{u}$. The excited-state mass is $59.9308\ \mathrm{u}+\Delta m=59.9322\ \mathrm{u}$.

perOption.A: Makes the excited state lighter than the ground state and uses too large a mass difference.
perOption.B: Subtracts the photon’s mass equivalent from the ground-state mass.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Adds a mass increment about twice that implied by the emitted photon energy.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
Antimony-124 undergoes radioactive decay, with a half-life of 60 days, to become tin-124. Tin-124 is stable.

Initially, a sample of antimony-124 contains no tin-124.

After what period of time will the ratio $\frac{\text{number of tin-124 nuclei}}{\text{number of antimony-124 nuclei}}$ equal 6?

A Between 60 days and 120 days
B 120 days
C Between 120 days and 180 days
D 180 days

stemImage.alt: Question 30: Antimony-124 undergoes radioactive decay, with a half-life of 60 days, to become tin-124. Tin-124 is stable. Initially, a sample of antimony-124 contains no tin

appearances.originalFile: grail:9648 SAJC 2022 Prelim P1 QP + Guide
YIJC/2026 JC2 H2 Prelim Paper 1 QP (Revised).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: It requires tracking the stable daughter nuclei as well as the undecayed parent nuclei.
questions.misconception: Taking the initial number of parent nuclei as the denominator

explanation.body: Tin-124 is stable, so after one $60$-day half-life the antimony-to-tin ratio is $1:1$. After two half-lives, $\tfrac14$ of the original antimony remains and $\tfrac34$ has become tin, so the ratio is $1:3$. After three half-lives the fractions are $\tfrac18$ and $\tfrac78$, giving $1:7$. The tin-to-antimony ratio therefore reaches $6$ between 120 and 180 days.

perOption.A: Between 60 and 120 days the ratio rises only from 1 to 3.
perOption.B: After 120 days the ratio is 3.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: After 180 days the ratio is 7.

A radioactive source contains two species. One has a half-life of 4 days and decays by the emission of alpha particles while the other has a half-life of 3 days and emits beta particles. The initial count-rate is 352 $\mathrm{min}^{-1}$, but when a sheet of paper is placed between the source and the detector this becomes 256 $\mathrm{min}^{-1}$. The background count-rate is 16 $\mathrm{min}^{-1}$.

What would be the count-rate without the paper present after 12 days?
questions.stemText: A radioactive source contains two species. One has a half-life of 4 days and decays by the emission of alpha particles while the other has a half-life of 3 days and emits beta particles. The initial count-rate is 352 min-1, but when a sheet of paper is placed between the source and the detector this becomes 256 min-1. The background count-rate is 16 min-1. What would be the count-rate without the paper present after 12 days? A 27 $\mathrm{min}^{-1}$ B 28 $\mathrm{min}^{-1}$ C 43 $\mathrm{min}^{-1}$ D 44 $\mathrm{min}^{-1}$

appearances.originalFile: grail:14539 (EJC) 2024 J2 H2 PRELIM QP P1

questions.difficultyReason: Requires isolating two count rates, applying different half-lives and restoring the background.
questions.misconception: Applying radioactive decay to the background count rate.

explanation.body: Subtracting background gives an initial source count rate of $352-16=336\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$. Paper blocks alpha particles, so their initial contribution is $352-256=96\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$, and the beta contribution is $336-96=240\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$. After 12 days, the total is $96(1/2)^{12/4}+240(1/2)^{12/3}+16=43\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Omits the background from the final count rate.
perOption.B: Adds less than the full background contribution to the decayed source count rate.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Includes background in the beta component before decay and adds background again at the end.

questions.stemText:
A radioactive source consists of $64\times10^{12}$ atoms of nuclide P of half-life 2 days. Another source consists of $8\times10^{12}$ atoms of nuclide Q of half-life 3 days. After how long will the number of undecayed nuclei in the two sources be equal?

A 6 days
B 9 days
C 12 days
D 18 days

questions.difficultyReason: It requires equating two decay laws with different half-lives and simplifying the powers.
questions.misconception: Confusing elapsed time with the number of half-lives

explanation.body: Set the surviving populations equal using $N=N_0(1/2)^{t/t_{1/2}}$. Cancelling the common factor of $10^{12}$ gives $64(1/2)^{t/2}=8(1/2)^{t/3}$, with $t$ in days. Thus $(1/2)^{t/2-t/3}=2^{3-6}$, so $t/6=3$ and $t=18$ days.

perOption.B: Allows for a difference of only 1.5 half-lives, leaving more P nuclei than Q nuclei.
perOption.C: Allows for a difference of only two half-lives, leaving twice as many P nuclei as Q nuclei.

B 8.8 MeV of energy is absorbed. C 8.8 MeV of energy is released. D 493 MeV of energy is absorbed. 493 MeV of energy is released.

questions.misconception: Confusing binding energy per nucleon with total binding energy

explanation.body: Iron-56 has 56 nucleons, so its total binding energy is $8.8\times56=492.8\ \mathrm{MeV}$. Forming the nucleus releases this energy, approximately $493\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

questions.stemText: Nuclear reaction: $^{235}_{92}\mathrm{U} + {}^1_0\mathrm{n} \to {}^{121}_{45}\mathrm{Rh} + {}^{113}_{47}\mathrm{Ag} + 2\,{}^1_0\mathrm{n}$. Binding energy per nucleon: U-235 = 7.59 MeV, Rh-121 = 8.26 MeV, Ag-113 = 8.52 MeV. What is the energy change in this reaction? A 73.9 MeV released. B 73.9 MeV absorbed. C 179 MeV released. D 179 MeV absorbed.

stemImage.alt: Question 29: Consider the following nuclear reaction: → 235 1 121 113 1 U + n Rh + Ag + 2 n 92 0 45 47 0 Data: 235 92U = 7.59 MeV binding energy per nucleon of binding energ

questions.difficultyReason: Needs total binding energy (per nucleon times nucleon number) and the sign convention for released versus absorbed.
questions.misconception: Confusing binding energy increase with energy absorbed

explanation.body:
Total binding energy before: $7.59\times235 = 1783.65\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

Total binding energy after: $(8.26\times121)+(8.52\times113) = 1962\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

Change in binding energy $= +179\ \mathrm{MeV}$, released as energy since the products are more stable. (The neutrons have no binding energy.)

perOption.A: Counts only part of the nucleons, or omits a product; gives 73.9 MeV.
perOption.B: Wrong magnitude and the wrong sense (absorbed).

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A radioactive source contains a radioisotope which has a half-life of 24 hours. In the absence of this source, a constant average count-rate of 10 $\mathrm{min}^{-1}$ is recorded. Immediately after the source is placed in a fixed position near the counter, the average count-rate rises to 90 $\mathrm{min}^{-1}$.

What average count-rate is expected with the source still in place 12 hours later?
questions.stemText: A radioactive source contains a radioisotope which has a half-life of 24 hours. In the absence of this source, a constant average count-rate of 10 min-1 is recorded. Immediately after the source is placed in a fixed position near the counter, the average count-rate rises to 90 min-1. What average count-rate is expected with the source still in place 12 hours later? A 45 $\mathrm{min}^{-1}$ B 50 $\mathrm{min}^{-1}$ C 57 $\mathrm{min}^{-1}$ D 67 $\mathrm{min}^{-1}$
questions.difficultyReason: Must subtract and re-add background count and handle a fractional half-life.
questions.misconception: Applying decay to the total count rate including background

explanation.body:
Initial true count rate from the source $= 90 - 10 = 80\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$.

Number of half-lives $= 12/24 = 0.5$, so $C = 80(1/2)^{0.5} = 57\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$.

Add back the background: final count $= 57 + 10 = 67\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Halves 90 directly, ignoring background and using one half-life.
perOption.B: Halves the source count after subtracting background (one full half-life, 40 + 10).
perOption.C: Gets the source count rate (57) but forgets to add back the background.
perOption.D: Correct. $57 + 10 = 67\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: A Geiger counter is placed near a radioactive source and different materials are placed between the source and the Geiger counter. The results of the tests are shown in the table. Material / count rate of Geiger counter per s: none 1000; paper 1000; aluminium foil 250; thick steel 50. What is the radiation emitted by the source? A $\alpha$ only; B $\alpha$ and $\gamma$; C $\alpha$ and $\beta$; D $\beta$ and $\gamma$.

stemImage.alt: Question 29: A Geiger counter is placed near a radioactive source and different materials are placed between the source and the Geiger counter. The results of the tests are

questions.difficultyReason: Standard penetrating-power reasoning from a short table.
questions.misconception: Assuming the radiation falling in intensity with a material proves that radiation type is absent.

explanation.body:
Paper does not reduce the count rate, so there is no $\alpha$ (which would not pass through paper).

$\beta$ is stopped by a few mm of aluminium, which is why the rate falls from 1000 to 250.

Only $\gamma$ can pass through thick steel, which is why a count remains (50 s$^{-1}$).

perOption.A: Alpha is absorbed by paper, but the rate is unchanged by paper.
perOption.B: No alpha: paper makes no difference. Aluminium reduces the count, so beta is present.
perOption.C: No alpha; and the count remaining behind thick steel shows gamma is present.
perOption.D: Correct. Beta (absorbed by aluminium) and gamma (penetrates steel).

questions.stem: The mass of the fuel in a fission reactor decreases at a rate of 6.0 × $10^{-6}$ kg $\mathrm{hour}^{-1}$. What is the maximum possible power output of the reactor?
questions.stemText: The mass of the fuel in a fission reactor decreases at a rate of 6.0 × 10−6 kg hour−1. What is the maximum possible power output of the reactor? A 75 MW B 150 MW C 300 MW D 9000 MW
questions.difficultyReason: Direct use of E = mc^2 with a unit conversion from hours to seconds.
questions.misconception: Forgetting to convert hours to seconds.

A radioactive source consists of a mixture of two isotopes P and Q.

P has a half-life of 60 minutes and Q has a half-life of 30 minutes. The initial count rate recorded by a suitable counter is $800\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$. After 120 minutes the counter registers a count rate of $80\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$.

What was the initial count rate of P?

A. $160\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$
B. $240\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$
C. $480\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$
D. $640\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$

stemImage.alt: Question 29: A radioactive source consists of a mixture of two isotopes P and Q. P has a half-life of 60 minutes and Q has a half-life of 30 minutes. The initial count rate

questions.difficultyReason: Combine two separate decay factors in simultaneous equations.
questions.misconception: Applying one half-life to the total count rate.

explanation.body: The initial rates satisfy $A_{P0}+A_{Q0}=800$. After 120 minutes, $A_{P0}(1/2)^{120/60}+A_{Q0}(1/2)^{120/30}=80$. Multiplying the resulting equation by 16 gives $4A_{P0}+A_{Q0}=1280$. Subtracting the initial-rate equation gives $3A_{P0}=480$, so $A_{P0}=160\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: This split predicts a final total of $60+35=95\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$.
perOption.C: Uses 480 before dividing by 3.
perOption.D: Gives the initial count rate of Q.

questions.misconception: Beta or gamma decay changes the mass number.

perOption.A: A mass-number loss of 33 is not divisible by 4.
perOption.B: Correct. The mass-number loss is 32.

binding energy per nucleon of $^{235}_{92}\mathrm{U}=7.59\ \mathrm{MeV}$
binding energy per nucleon of $^{121}_{45}\mathrm{Rh}=8.26\ \mathrm{MeV}$
binding energy per nucleon of $^{113}_{47}\mathrm{Ag}=8.52\ \mathrm{MeV}$

What is the energy released during this fission process?

A $9.19\ \mathrm{MeV}$
B $24.4\ \mathrm{MeV}$
C $73.9\ \mathrm{MeV}$

questions.misconception: Binding energies per nucleon can be subtracted directly to get the energy released.

perOption.B: Underestimates the gain by failing to account for the full change in nuclear binding energy.
perOption.C: Undercounts the binding-energy gain of the two daughter nuclei.
perOption.D: Correct.

30 A radioactive source emits radiation of type X.
A counter is placed at a fixed position close to the source.
When a piece of paper is placed between the counter and the source, the average count rate is 24 counts per minute.
When the paper is removed, the average count rate is 532 counts per minute.
What is radiation X and the average count rate immediately after two half-lives?
[Table: radiation X | count rate after two half-lives / min$^{-1}$]
A $\alpha$ | 127
B $\beta$ | 127
C $\alpha$ | 151
D $\beta$ | 151

stemImage.alt: Question 30: A radioactive source emits radiation of type X. A counter is placed at a fixed position close to the source. When a piece of paper is placed between the counter

questions.difficultyReason: Requires identifying background count and correcting for it before and after halving.
questions.misconception: applying half-life decay to the background count

explanation.body:
The count rate drops sharply when paper is inserted, so the radiation is stopped by paper: it must be $\alpha$ radiation, which has low penetrating power.

The remaining $24\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$ is the background count rate, so the initial count rate due to the source is $532 - 24 = 508\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$.

After two half-lives the source count rate is $\tfrac{1}{4}(508) = 127\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$, so the reading is $127 + 24 = 151\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Correct radiation, but forgets to add the background count back to the reading.
perOption.B: $\beta$ radiation would not be stopped by paper, and the background is not added back.
perOption.C: Correct. $\alpha$; $\tfrac{1}{4}(532-24) + 24 = 151\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$.
perOption.D: $\beta$ radiation would pass through paper.

questions.stemText:
The graph shows the variation with time $t$ of the activity $A$ of a pure sample of a radioactive nuclide. The total energy released due to radioactive decay of the sample in time $T$ is $E$. The area of the shaded portion is $S$.

[Graph of $A/\mathrm{Bq}$ against $t/\mathrm{s}$. The curve starts above zero at $t=0$ and falls, becoming less steep. The area under the curve from $0$ to $T$ is shaded.]

What does the quantity $E/S$ represent?
A The number of decays which occur in time $T$
B The average power due to radioactive decay
C The average energy produced in time $T$
D The energy released for each radioactive decay

explanation.body: Activity $A$ is the number of decays per unit time, so the shaded area $S$ is the total number of decays in time $T$. Dividing the total energy $E$ by that count gives the energy released per radioactive decay.

questions.stem: A detector placed close to a radioactive source measures an activity of 320 Bq. The background activity at this location is 20 Bq. The radioactive nuclide has a half-life of 12 hours. What activity is measured after 9 hours?
questions.stemText: A detector placed close to a radioactive source measures an activity of 320 Bq. The background activity at this location is 20 Bq. The radioactive nuclide has a half-life of 12 hours. What activity is measured after 9 hours? A 178 Bq B 198 Bq C 225 Bq D 245 Bq
questions.difficultyReason: Requires subtracting background, applying a fractional half-life, and restoring background for the measured reading.
questions.misconception: Applying radioactive decay to the background count

explanation.body: The initial background-corrected activity is $320-20=300\,\mathrm{Bq}$. After nine hours the corrected activity is $300(1/2)^{9/12}\approx178\,\mathrm{Bq}$. The observed reading includes background, giving $178+20=198\,\mathrm{Bq}$.

perOption.A: Leaves out the background when converting the decayed source activity into the detector reading.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Overestimates the remaining source activity even before correcting for the background in the detector reading.
perOption.D: Adding background to an overestimated source activity of 225 Bq still gives too high a reading.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
It is observed that α-particles incident on a thin gold foil are mostly undeflected, while a small proportion of them are deflected at very large angles.

Which statement provides the explanation for these observations?

A The α-particles are scattered by electrons.
B The α-particles are diffracted by the crystal lattice.
C The α-particles collide with small but massive nuclei.
D The α-particles undergo nuclear fission.

stemImage.alt: Question 29: It is observed that -particles incident on a thin gold foil are mostly undeflected, while a small proportion of them are deflected at very large angles. Which

questions.difficultyReason: Direct recall of the conclusion of Rutherford's scattering experiment.

explanation.body:
Most α-particles pass through undeflected or with only small deflections, so the chance of an α-particle getting close to the positive charge is small: the atom is mostly empty space.

A small fraction (<1%) are deflected through large angles, and a few bounce back close to 180°. Such large deflections need a large force, so all the positive charge must be concentrated in a nucleus that is tiny compared with the atom.

Hence the nucleus is small and very massive.

perOption.A: Electrons are far too light to deflect a massive α-particle through large angles.
perOption.B: Diffraction by the lattice would give a regular pattern, not rare large-angle scattering; the effect is due to Coulomb repulsion by nuclei.
perOption.C: Correct. A small, massive, positive nucleus explains both observations.
perOption.D: Fission is not involved; the α-particles are simply scattered.

questions.stem:
A radioactive sample is placed in a vacuum together with a Geiger Muller (GM) tube. The GM tube is placed 10 cm from the sample and the initial count rate is 1000 $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. Several materials are then placed between the sample and GM tube, and the results are shown below.

What radiation is being emitted by the sample?
questions.stemText: A radioactive sample is placed in a vacuum together with a Geiger Muller (GM) tube. The GM tube is placed 10 cm from the sample and the initial count rate is 1000 s–1. Several materials are then placed between the sample and GM tube, and the results are shown below. count rate / s–1 material 0.1 mm aluminium sheet 500 7 mm aluminium sheet 500 10 cm of lead near zero What radiation is being emitted by the sample? A alpha radiation only B beta radiation only C beta and gamma radiation D alpha and gamma radiation
questions.difficultyReason: Requires interpreting count-rate data against known penetrating powers, a standard exercise.
questions.misconception: Thinking a few mm of aluminium does not stop β

explanation.body:
Typical stopping materials: α is stopped by about $10^{-2}$ mm of aluminium or a few cm of air; β by about 5 mm of aluminium; γ by about 100 mm of lead.

The 0.1 mm aluminium sheet halves the count rate, so α radiation must be present and is blocked by the sheet.

The 7 mm aluminium sheet has no further effect, so β radiation is absent.

The 10 cm of lead reduces the count rate to nearly zero, so γ radiation must be present.

perOption.A: With α only, the 0.1 mm aluminium would stop everything; 500 counts per second still get through until the lead.
perOption.B: β would be stopped by 7 mm of aluminium, but the count rate is unchanged from 0.1 mm to 7 mm.
perOption.C: β would be stopped by the 7 mm sheet, and something must be stopped by 0.1 mm of aluminium (only α is).
perOption.D: Correct. α is stopped by thin aluminium; γ passes through aluminium and is stopped by thick lead.

What is the number of neutrons for the lead (Pb) nuclide?

questions.stemText:
Which of the following statements is true?

A $\alpha$ particles can be stopped by $1\ \mathrm{m}$ of lead.
B $\beta$ particles can be deflected when travelling parallel to a magnetic field.
C $\gamma$ particles can be stopped by paper.
D $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$ particles are all charged particles.

stemImage.alt: Question 29: Which of the following statements is true?

questions.difficultyReason: The item checks familiar radiation properties and the condition for a magnetic force.
questions.misconception: Assuming any charged particle in a magnetic field is deflected

explanation.body: A thin sheet of paper can stop $\alpha$ particles, so $1\ \mathrm{m}$ of lead can stop them too. A $\beta$ particle travelling parallel to a magnetic field feels zero magnetic force. Gamma rays penetrate paper and are uncharged electromagnetic radiation.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: A $\beta$ particle needs a velocity component across the field to experience a magnetic force.
perOption.C: Paper provides negligible shielding for gamma rays, which require thick shielding such as lead.
perOption.D: Gamma rays are uncharged electromagnetic radiation.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Technetium-99 has a half life of 6.0 hrs. It is used as a biological tracer. A sample of technetium-99 with an activity of 8.0 x $10^{10}$ Bq is injected into the bloodstream of a patient. 20 hours later, when the technetium-99 is assumed to be uniformly distributed throughout the blood of the patient, a 10 $\mathrm{cm}^{3}$ blood sample is obtained. The activity from the sample is found to be 1.6 x $10^{7}$ Bq.

What is the total volume of blood in the patient?
questions.stemText: Technetium-99 has a half life of 6.0 hrs. It is used as a biological tracer. A sample of technetium-99 with an activity of 8.0 x 1010 Bq is injected into the bloodstream of a patient. 20 hours later, when the technetium-99 is assumed to be uniformly distributed throughout the blood of the patient, a 10 cm3 blood sample is obtained. The activity from the sample is found to be 1.6 x 107 Bq. What is the total volume of blood in the patient? A 3100 $\mathrm{cm}^{3}$ B 4700 $\mathrm{cm}^{3}$ C 5000 $\mathrm{cm}^{3}$ D 6300 $\mathrm{cm}^{3}$
questions.difficultyReason: The student must calculate the decayed activity and scale from the blood sample to the total volume.
questions.misconception: Scaling from the initial activity

explanation.body: After $20\ \mathrm{h}$, the total activity is $A=A_0e^{-\lambda t}=8.0\times10^{10}e^{-(\ln 2)(20/6.0)}=7.937\times10^9\ \mathrm{Bq}$. With the tracer uniformly distributed, the volume ratio equals the activity ratio. Thus $V/10=(7.937\times10^9)/(1.6\times10^7)$, giving about $5000\ \mathrm{cm^3}$.

perOption.A: This volume implies too little activity after 20 h.
perOption.B: This volume underestimates the ratio of total activity to sample activity.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: This volume overestimates the ratio of total activity to sample activity.
